translations.text: THE HEAVENS REJOICE when stars rise among stars, and harbors when small ships gleam among great ships, and when clouds play up and down among clouds and scatter showers of sweet dew. The church also rejoices when congregations hasten after congregations and feasts press upon feasts in the holy places. They do not change their powers according to the places, but renew their affection as the places change: from blessing to blessing, from church to church. Rather, we ought to say, in the Apostle’s words, from faith to faith and from glory to glory. And the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “They shall go from strength to strength.” Yesterday the royal crown of the apostles made us radiant, and today the crown of the martyrs enlightens us. The church receives both the royal crown and the victor’s crown, and in it the prophet’s saying is fulfilled: “The church is a crown of beauty in the Lord’s hand, and a royal diadem in the hand of God.” May our bosoms be crowned with the labors of these martyrs, and the walls of this temple with the lights of lamps, both a rampart and a bulwark. A double bulwark from the Trinity has been placed around us, for nothing in heaven or on earth can be enlightened without the Holy Trinity. These new things imitate the original pattern, for what God does invisibly, these lamps do visibly: this illumination has surrounded us like a bulwark. For he promises, “I will be a wall of fire around my people.”

Truly, the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, like abundant waters covering the seas. Even now, through the holy congregations, the prophet’s hidden saying is fulfilled: “The earth is the Lord’s, with all its fullness.” The prophets proclaimed this, but they did not speak these words with reference to the present established state of things. Who does not know that the earth is the Lord’s, with all its fullness? Or who doubts whether another lord has a share in creation? For all of us, believers and unbelievers alike, plainly know through long-established habit that everything belongs to God. But the prophets did not say this with reference to the present established state of things, but with reference to the former error, when idolatry [?] the earth, when people burned with zeal for images, when God was not recognized and those who were not gods received worship.

When, as the Apostle says, “They worshiped the creation and not the Creator,” the holy prophets saw the earth as though driven into exile by some tyrant. They cried out to those who had gone astray: “The earth is the Lord’s, with all its fullness. Why do you wander in error? Why do you reckon the regions of the earth to belong to various gods?” For the places were named after the demons. Just as a rebel invades by force and drives out another’s kingdom for his own sake, so the demons entered the world and seized its various regions for themselves. Some were called gods of the Lycians, some of the people of Attica, others of the [?], and others of the Achaeans. Each was allotted its own region, and the places were named after the designation of the gods to whom they were dedicated. For example, the Athenians were named after the god whom they worshiped, and Heliopolis after its own god, and each people after its own gods. To avoid lengthening this account by listing them, the places too were named after the gods.

And so that the earlier account may not mislead you in any way, pay attention to the writings that agree with it. The ancients thought that each of the gods had received one region of the earth, and that God possessed the region of Judea. For the Assyrian himself said, when they came against the land of the Palestinians, “Did their gods save their respective countries, that the God of Israel should save you?” The ancients thought that the Lord of all was one of those supposed gods. And just as each of those falsely called gods received his own country, so God possessed the country of the Palestinians as his own particular domain. As the other barbarian also said, he had authority only over the mountains of the Palestinians.

Now, to those misguided people who divided the earth from its one sovereign and reckoned the regions under heaven to be under many dominions, they cried out, “The earth, with all its fullness, belongs to the Lord.” Then, as though required to make clear why the whole earth belongs to the Lord, he brings forward the familiar facts of creation to establish the extent of his dominion. “He himself,” he says, “laid its foundations upon the sea and established it upon the rivers.”

From then on, the whole earth was filled with the glory of Christ, and the whole earth became full of the knowledge of the Lord. As the prophet Isaiah says, “Like the many waters that cover the seas.” The laws of faith establish a rule that nature does not admit. You know, brothers, that many rivers from every region under heaven flow into the seas, yet they have not covered them. Rather, they themselves have been covered, and have not covered the seas. But the new proclamation promises a new kind of power. “The knowledge of God,” he says, “filled the earth like the many waters that cover the seas.” What cannot happen by nature, he establishes through knowledge. Just as the sea cannot be covered by waters from elsewhere, so, according to the ordinary course of things, the earth cannot be filled with knowledge. But look: the word has spread and filled all the ends of the earth, and the teaching of the gospel has covered the seas.

Which sea? The one in which people were tossed about as in an abyss. The word of God went forth and filled every region under heaven. And what Daniel said was fulfilled: “The stone that was cut from the mountain without hands became a great mountain, and the whole earth was filled by it.” At times he compares it to waters that cover everything under heaven, for the teaching advanced on its course, and the word fills the ends of the earth; and at times to a mountain, because of the height of the teaching, because its speech about God reaches heaven. “In the last days,” he says, “the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, and the house of God above the summits of the mountains.”

Which house? The church. For it is not built upon mountains, but stands established in the height of its speech about God. The church is the house of God, as Paul writes to Timothy: “So that you may know,” he says, “how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the church.” And why is it upon the mountains? The Savior says, “A city standing upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

There was a stone that was cut out without hands, for Christ was born without a man. The stone was cut out without hands, for Christ was born without marital union. And the stone became a great mountain and filled everything beneath heaven. But lest anyone consider these words forced and say, “What connection does a stone have with establishing a birth in the flesh?” we must also make it clear that human offspring are called stones hewn from rock. From this it will be established that being cut out means being born. The prophet Isaiah says to the people, “Look to the solid rock from which you were hewn.” And to explain the rock, he adds, “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah, who gave birth to you.” Do you see that he calls human offspring stones hewn from rock?

And why does he speak of the people's offspring as coming from a rock? Because Sarah was barren. A rock too is barren and bears no fruit. He calls her a rock because she was barren by nature but able to bear children by grace. “Look,” he says, “to the rock from which you were hewn.” Just as the stones hewn from rock there signify the people's offspring, so here the stone cut out without hands signifies Christ's birth in the flesh. And see how carefully he speaks. For rocks often break off and fall from mountains without hands, but he did not say that it broke off or split apart, but that it was cut out. Since he was to speak of the birth ordained by divine providence, he says, “The stone was cut out without hands.” For he was not born according to the laws of nature, but through a new kind of travail [?], and without experience of marital union the flower blossomed from a virgin womb. And it became a great mountain and filled the earth. If the events did not agree with the words, then this defense is in vain, and we are trying to force the truth by falsehood. But if the events shine forth and cry aloud before the words, and the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of Christ, then, if we are ungrateful for the benefits of these accomplishments, we too shall hear from the Lord, “Even if you are silent, these stones will cry out.” A stone was cut out without hands and became a great mountain. And all peoples hasten to this mountain and say, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.”

And pay close attention to how he first announces the conversion of the Gentiles and then the calling of the Jews. For first some of the Gentiles believe in Christ, and after them some of the Jews. “Many nations will follow and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and he will tell us his ways, and we will walk with him.’” And what does he add after this? “For the law,” he says, “will go forth from Zion.” See how he announces the law of the second covenant, for the first law came not from Zion but from Mount Sinai. “The law,” he says, “will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he will judge among the nations”—and the other things that follow, one by one. When he has foretold the conversion of the Gentiles, the prophetic Spirit then calls out to the Jews and says, “And now, house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord.” Do you see? First the Gentiles believe, and then the Jewish people are called.

You have the example of Joseph. The foreshadowings of the giver of life were fulfilled beforehand: Joseph first ruled in Egypt, and then over his ungrateful brothers; he first ruled over the Egyptians, who were foreigners, and then over his brothers, who were of his own people. And see the wonders: will not everything that David said be fulfilled completely in Christ? “He established it,” he says, “as a testimony in Joseph.” This is another way of saying that he placed in Joseph a prophecy that would bear witness. If Joseph had stayed with his father Jacob, Egypt would not have received the one who would provide for it. Pay close attention: if Joseph had remained there, cherished by his father, Egypt would not have received its guardian, the one who devised a remedy for the famine. Joseph was sent to visit his brothers and the flocks; the Only-begotten was sent into the world to seek the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Dreams adorned Joseph, and miracles glorified Christ. “I saw that my brothers and I were reaping, and their sheaves bowed down to my sheaf.” Since they would bow down because of the danger of famine, God showed beforehand, through the sheaves of grain, the outcome of the events to come. First the sheaves bowed down to him, because first his brothers would bow down to him. The circumstances of the famine first brought them down to Egypt, and on the second occasion they recognized their brother. The first time they stood trembling before him as before a ruler; on the second occasion they recognized him and were honored. They recognized him and were glorified as the brothers of the glorified Joseph.

The brothers hated Joseph because of his dreams, and they did not know that they were hating not him but the one who showed him the dreams. Surely he did not see the dream by his own will! Therefore, whoever fought against the dreamer was fighting against God. But see how wickedness blinds people! Why do you fight against this dreamer? Will the outcomes of these dreams prove true or false? If they prove true, by what devices can you set aside the truth? And if they prove false, why should you envy this person who babbles about his nighttime fancies? Joseph went to visit his brothers, to show an act of love, and they repaid his kindness with the insult of ingratitude. He spoke words of peace to them, but they gathered for conflict and fought against him, so that the saying of the giver of life might be fulfilled: “They hated me without cause.” See the wonders: “The dreamer is coming,” they say. The dream’s vision terrified them—or rather, not the vision, but the fear that these things would come to pass. They plotted the holy man’s death, and God made their wickedness into an instrument of providence. For it is God’s work not only to bestow gifts of his own, but also to turn our wickedness to good use. They wanted to kill their brother. Reuben offered good counsel: “Let us not kill him, for he is our brother and our flesh. Instead, let us throw him into one of the pits somewhere.” He had it in mind to find a way to save him, but in fact he was carrying out the work of providence. Joseph was not killed, but went down alive into the pit, for he was a foreshadowing of the living one who descended alive into Hades. Joseph went down into the pit, and the pit was empty of water: a likeness of the tomb of the giver of life, which was empty of the dead.

Joseph was thrown into the pit. Judah, moved with pity for his brother, put forward a good proposal: not to kill him in the pit. “What profit would there be if we killed him? Come, let us sell him.” Judah spared his brother out of concern, but the all-knowing God was carrying out the work of providence. Joseph had to be sold at that time through Judah, because the Life-giver too was sold through Judas the betrayer. The Ishmaelites took him and brought him to Egypt. By what means? By camel. And what were the camels carrying? Resin, [?], and incense. Indeed, it was fitting to send [?] oil in its humiliation along with incense. We can understand from the account itself how wickedness unwillingly praises the one being sold, so that they may receive a higher price. The Ishmaelites asked, “Is this young man good?” They were compelled to comply, for they saw the silver in their hands. “He is freeborn,” they said, “and noble. He does not know how to steal; he cannot swear falsely.” Willingly, against its will, wickedness exposed its own falsehood.

Joseph went down to Egypt, because the Life-giver too was to go to Egypt. Joseph was sold to foreigners; Christ was handed over to the Gentiles: “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of the Gentiles.” Joseph was in the hands of the Ishmaelites, and Jesus in the hands of the Gentiles. Joseph went down to Egypt and was afflicted at first, for Jesus too was not accepted by the Gentiles at first, and afterward they worshiped the one whom they had persecuted and insulted. The image was accurately depicted in Joseph’s suffering from the lust of winter [?]. The woman seized Joseph’s clothes, just as death seized the Life-giver’s body. Joseph stripped off his clothes and left them with the wanton woman, just as the Life-giver, when he rose, left his clothes in the tomb. Joseph entered prison, because Christ too was to enter the tomb. Joseph was ruler over the prisoners, because Christ too is king of the living and the dead.

And see the nobility of his spirit. Outwardly he was in prison and in chains; the free man was in slavery, and the man destined to be honored with kingship was in prison. He never doubted like someone weak in faith. He did not say, “What of the dreams [?]? Where are the false visions? Where are God’s foretelling declarations? You promised me kingship, yet I am compelled to serve. You promised to give me authority as a gift, yet I do not even enjoy the freedom common to everyone. I descended from freedom into slavery; I went from ease into prison.” He entertained no such thought, but persevered and awaited the fulfillment of events. And who will testify that he looked forward to the fulfillment of events and did not doubt? There were, it says, two servants of Pharaoh in the prison. They had dreams and were sad. Joseph said to them, “Why are you sad?” And they said, “We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them.” He did not say, “Let no one pay attention to dreams. Let my dreams serve as an example of other dreams.” Instead, to make it clear that he was intent on the fulfillment of his own dreams, he said, “Tell me, and I will explain them to you.” Have your own dreams come to pass at all, that you should interpret those of others? He interprets their dreams and looks forward to the fulfillment of his own.

Pay close attention; turn from the figure to the reality. If you wish to learn about Joseph’s character, do not learn it from his brothers, for envy conceals the truth and casts the free man into slavery. Nor from the Ishmaelites, for they too bought the free man as a slave. Nor from his mistress, for she slandered him because of her own shamelessness. But if you wish to understand what sort of person Joseph was, ask his father, and he says, “He is a son, and a beloved son.”

Come to Christ. If you wish to understand what sort of person Christ is, do not learn it from the Jews, for envy disguises the truth. Nor from the idolaters, for they hate the destroyer of their images. Nor from the schismatics, because just as the Ishmaelites did not know that they had bought a free man, so the schismatics do not recognize him, and therefore make the free man a slave. Nor from the Jews, for they are enemies of the cross. Nor from the idolaters, for they hate the one who exposes their idols. Nor from the heretics, for they are like Ishmael, who was not born of the free woman but of the slave woman. The Ishmaelites are a figure of the schismatics, and the children of the free woman are a figure of believers.

When the patriarch blessed Joseph, he said, “Your blessing is from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth.” Pay attention: these are God’s gifts, bestowed from heaven and earth. The gifts were not given to Ishmael, for he did not possess them. “By the sword,” he says, “you shall live.” The Ishmaelites have no other occupation by which they can make any profit, except the sword alone. Like them are the schismatics, who believe neither the declarations from heaven nor the prophets, but bring the sword against them. And fittingly so, for they are Ishmaelites: they live not by the word of God, but by the sword of folly.

From now on, do not learn what Christ is like from Jews, idolaters, or heretics. Instead, if you wish to understand, learn his characteristics from his own root. See what his Father testifies about him: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” The Father calls him Son, and do you call him a creature? “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son.” And again: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” Does the Father not convince you? Do the declarations of the prophets not make you stand in awe? Do the ranks of the apostles not inspire reverence in you? Let the demons put you to shame. For you heed neither the Father, who says, “This is my beloved Son,” nor Paul, who proclaims, “You are the Son of the living God,” nor Isaiah, who calls him mighty God. You have denied the Scriptures; at least show some reverence before the demons. Matthew says: “Demons came out of many people and cried out, ‘You are the Son of God.’” Likewise, Mark says that they agreed in their words and said: “We know who you are, the Son of God.” Likewise, Luke declares that when the demons saw him, they fell down before him, cried out, and said: “We know who you are, the Son of God. [?] before the time to judge us.” The demons confess him as the Son of God, and do you call him a creature? You are in great distress, for you make the demons appear more righteous than yourself: an abundance of evil makes those with less evil appear righteous. For this reason, because of Jerusalem’s abundance of evil, he said to her: “Sodom has been shown to be more righteous than you.” This was another way of saying: “Compared with your sins, the city of the Sodomites appeared righteous.”

You have the example; bow down before the truth. For if Joseph had not gone to Egypt, the land of the Egyptians would have died of hunger. And if the giver of life had not come into the world, the whole world would have died from hunger for the divine word. And to learn that God, the divine Word, is food, listen: “Behold, I will send you not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord.” Oh, what wonders! How the example was depicted beforehand in the prophet! You have seen the example in Joseph; see also the example of the resurrection in Daniel. They cast Daniel into the pit, against the will of Darius and Cyrus. Christ went up onto the cross with Pilate’s reluctant consent. The united body of officials compelled King Darius, and the united body of Jews compelled Pilate. Darius went early to see the pit and Daniel, to find out whether he was safe. The apostles and the women went early to the tomb to see whether the living one was alive.

Turn, heretics, from unbelief to faith. Do not be worse than water. Water saw Jesus and became wine; yet you say “Son” and call him a servant. He performed his first sign in Cana of Galilee, so that the saying might be fulfilled: “Galilee of the Gentiles—the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.” The first sign took place at a wedding, because the human race first increases through marriage, and a wedding is the root of the human plant. He blesses the root so that he may bless its shoots. And I marvel at this: not merely that he was invited and agreed to go, but that he went not to some distinguished house where a wedding was taking place, but to a wedding in the house of a poor man. The man in whose house the wedding took place was poor—so poor that even the little wine ran out. He was poor in possessions, but became rich in the treasures of truth.

The Lord appeared and changed the water into wine. His mother reminded him: “They have no wine,” she said. She was his mother according to the flesh and his servant according to his divinity. She was his servant according to his divine nature and became his mother according to the arrangement of his incarnation. He was both her God and her son: her God according to his lordship, and her son according to the arrangement of his incarnation. “They have no wine.” “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” At this point some understood him to be promising something different. But he was reproaching his mother, because she still regarded the Lord of mankind as a mere man. He rebuked her, not because she reminded him, but because she reminded him as though he were a man. Many thought that “My hour has not yet come” meant, “The time for miracles has not yet come.” But if it had not come, how could you perform the miracle? Rather, he was reproaching his mother for reminding him needlessly and at an unsuitable time, and because God has no need to be reminded. “The time for my revelation has not yet come, for no one yet knows who I am.” And so that you may learn that he said those words not to [?] the miracle, but because she had called attention to his power, his mother, understanding his dignity, said: “Do whatever he tells you.”

He spoke and changed the water into wine—he who turns water into oil. For through the olive tree he turns dew into oil, and through [?] into wheat, and through other plants into aromatic herbs, and through trees into fruit; and in all things he gives every plant its own flavor. There is one rain, but many different flavors are produced. Do not marvel only because he changed water into wine. Rather, marvel greatly because throughout creation he turns the same rain into different colors and flavors, and blood into milk, and all these things, too, into their own colors and flavors. Through daily familiarity people treated his great works with contempt, while something new in an unexpected act of his providence seemed marvelous. Otherwise, why do you not marvel at how he turns blood in women’s breasts into the white substance of milk? Why are you not astonished that he changes dark hair into white, something that the skill of dyers is wholly unable to accomplish? It is possible to dye something white black, but to make something black white is utterly impossible. Blood cannot be dyed, nor can something once dyed red be turned white. Yet he turns dark blood into white blood and changes black hair into white hair, so that you may learn that nature does not bring this about by itself; rather, he established the rule that nature should be this way.

So when you see him going to a wedding and making water into wine, marvel. But know that these are only tastes of his great works. It is great, though not in comparison with the wonder-worker; rather, we enjoy it because of his love. It is therefore right and fitting to understand that the miracles of the giver of life were very small in relation to him, but very great for those who benefited from them. Moses bears witness that this is so when he recounts to them the miracles performed in the land of the Egyptians: “Remember how the Lord your God brought you out of the land of the Egyptians with great signs and awesome deeds.” See how he marveled at the miracles. See also how the worker of miracles considers the deeds small: “I did all these things to the Egyptians so that you might tell your children’s children how I played with the Egyptians.” Do you see? What seems miraculous to us is play to God. But enough of this for now.

May the light of Christ dawn upon us, and may the divine word illuminate our souls, so that we may strip off the works of darkness and put on the works of light, make our preaching shine through our words, and adorn with our deeds the promise we have made; so that through words, deeds, and faith, and with God's approval, we may send up glory to the all-holy Trinity forever. Amen.
